pack.title: Sihtric's penny: a king and Dublin on silver

presentation.era: late tenth to early eleventh century
presentation.anchor: Sihtric Silkbeard · Dublin mint · first locally struck silver penny
presentation.question: What kind of port needs a mint, and what does a king make travel when he puts his name and city on silver?
presentation.opening: Six chapters move from the connected port through Sihtric's authority, exchange and mint motive, the hammered penny, its provisional legend, and a named specimen found at Glendalough.
presentation.evidenceLimit: The pack uses museum objects, numismatic synthesis, archaeology and bounded historical context. It does not invent a mint decree, a continuous market scene, Sihtric's exact likeness, universal penny use or the coin's missing route.
presentation.sourceTitle: NMI silver penny of SITRIC REX DUBLIN and the earliest Dublin coinage
presentation.sourceDetail: Claims D01–D06 and D09 · exact learner-facing type, both-face legend and catalogue reading remain behind numismatist review
presentation.artifactPrompt: Carry obverse, reverse, legend expansion, date range and the missing route to Glendalough together.
presentation.tegCanDo: Recognise and produce supported Irish for place, exchange, handling, names and past movement inside an object-led city story.

chapters.title: An Calafort roimh an Mionta · The port before the mint

pages.title: A port before an Irish mint
pages.context: Baile Átha Cliath · late tenth century
pages.body: Before Dublin struck its own coins, it was already a baile and a cathair connected by the abhainn, the sea and every arriving long. Imported silver and foreign coins circulated through a port whose market did not wait for a local mint to become active.
pages.detail: The mint is a consequence of an urban trading world, not the event that creates Dublin from nothing.
pages.visualCaption: Generated editorial interpretation of Dublin's dark pool and port · not documentary evidence

pages.title: Money arrived before local coinage
pages.body: For roughly a century, Dublin's Viking inhabitants used coins struck elsewhere alongside weighed silver and other forms of value. A local penny therefore entered a practice of exchange that was already familiar with distant designs and metal standards.
pages.detail: The story avoids a false switch from barter to money on one dramatic day.

displayItems.title: Weighed silver

pages.title: Two place-names hold different water
pages.body: Dubhlinn joins dubh — black — to linn — pool. Baile Átha Cliath points to the settlement at the ford of the hurdles. The names do not reduce to one neat founding label; they preserve different relationships to water and crossing within the city.
pages.detail: The language lens belongs to real place-names, not decorative etymology.

pages.title: The sea makes the city outward-facing
pages.body: Ships tied Dublin to towns and rulers around the Irish Sea and beyond. Cargo, people, coin types and political news could all travel along the same routes. The local mint would borrow from that connected world rather than announce independence from it.
pages.detail: Connection explains imitation: a familiar coin design could be more useful than a wholly novel one.

pages.body: Archaeology and coin finds support a substantial port and market. They do not preserve one camera-ready day in which every route, language and commodity appears together. The chapter establishes conditions rather than staging an invented market crowd.
pages.detail: The city is real; the composite street scene stays outside the evidence claim.

pages.title: A local mint becomes imaginable
pages.context: Chapter turn · port to royal decision
pages.body: A city that receives ships, foreign silver and recognisable coin types has the material and social ground for local minting. The next chapter asks who could put a name on that silver and make the city's authority travel.
pages.detail: The change is not from no money to money, but from imported coinage to a local royal issue.

pages.title: Sihtric rules a connected city
pages.body: The rí at the centre of the first coinage is Sihtric, often called Silkbeard. His baile, cathair and linn dubh depended on long, abhainn and sea routes already in motion. A mint offered a new way to join the king's ainm to airgead moving through Dublin's trádáil and margadh.
pages.detail: The previous chapter's place words return as the political setting for a named ruler.

pages.title: Norse rule and Irish ties overlap
pages.body: Sihtric belonged to the Uí Ímair ruling dynasty and governed a city with deep Norse, Irish and Irish Sea connections. Annal traditions and later histories place him inside changing alliances rather than a simple foreign-versus-Irish line.
pages.detail: The chapter keeps biography to what the coin story needs: named ruler, connected city and authority expressed through minting.

pages.title: A name can travel farther than a body
pages.body: A ruler's name on a coin moves through hands and places the ruler will never visit. Sihtric's issues made his authority portable while naming the city that produced them. The object joins person and place in a few compressed letters.
pages.detail: The coin is not a portrait biography. It is an issued object carrying names, type and authority.

pages.title: A legend claims authority; it does not prove total control
pages.body: Putting a royal name on coinage is evidence of minting authority and ambition. It does not show that every payment in Dublin used the new pennies or that Sihtric controlled every route from which silver arrived.
pages.detail: The object's strong claim remains bounded by the uneven reach of early coin circulation.

pages.title: The coin anchors the biography
pages.body: Later fame connects Sihtric to Clontarf and a long reign. This county account stays with the mint because the coin itself can be inspected and read. Biography enters only where it explains the authority behind that issue.
pages.detail: The object prevents a whole reign from becoming a hurried historical montage.

pages.title: Authority needs metal, labour and a reason
pages.body: A king and city can be named on silver, but the decision to mint still needs material and purpose. The next chapter enters the market to ask what locally struck money could do—and which answers are evidence rather than inference.
pages.detail: The question shifts from who can issue a coin to why an issue becomes useful.

chapters.title: Cén Fáth Mionta? · Why a mint?

pages.title: Silver becomes a local instrument
pages.body: The rí and his ainm return on airgead, a word that can mean money or silver. In Sihtric's margadh and trádáil, people could ceannaigh, díol, tabhair and tóg—buy, sell, give and take. A local penny made those actions carry a royal and urban mark.
pages.detail: The market words return the mint to ordinary exchange without pretending every transaction used one standard object.
pages.visualCaption: Generated editorial interpretation of a Dublin riverside market · not documentary evidence

pages.title: A mint may serve more than shopping
pages.body: Scholars infer that coinage could help rulers pay followers and display authority as well as support exchange. The surviving penny cannot tell us which motive came first in Sihtric's mind. It shows the issue; motive remains a reasoned interpretation.
pages.detail: The interface marks mint motive as inference rather than turning it into a recorded royal speech.

pages.title: A small object makes authority repeatable
pages.body: A coin can be counted, weighed, tested and passed. Each exchange repeats its design and letters. The power of the penny lies less in a single ceremony than in ordinary handling: give it, take it, spend it, receive it.
pages.detail: The learning interaction follows the object's real affordance—handling—without pretending the learner is present in the tenth-century market.

pages.title: The penny does not preserve a market price list
pages.body: The first issues establish local minting, not a complete table of what one penny bought in Dublin. Values varied by time, quality and context. The chapter therefore practises exchange language without attaching invented prices to food or cargo.
pages.detail: A tempting shopping simulation would create false precision around an uncertain economy.

pages.title: Recognisable silver still varied in the hand
pages.body: A penny type offered a recognisable denomination and design, but individual coins could vary in strike, wear and weight. Trust came from a wider practice of testing and recognition rather than from modern machine uniformity.
pages.detail: Exact metrology belongs to the selected specimen and numismatist review; this chapter keeps the practical point without inventing figures.

pages.title: The mint is fact; its full motive is not
pages.body: The earliest issues prove that coinage was struck in Dublin under Sihtric. Market support, payment and royal display are plausible functions. The draft presents them as interpretations whose weight a numismatist and historian must review.
pages.detail: The story keeps the question alive instead of closing it with an invented decree.

pages.body: Whatever mix of exchange, payment and display motivated the issue, the answer survives as silver. The next chapter stops asking what a mint might do and examines what this penny is: material, type, date and manufacture.
pages.detail: Interpretation gives way to object description.

chapters.title: An Chéad Phingin · The first penny

pages.title: The first locally struck penny
pages.body: The exchange actions ceannaigh, díol, tabhair and tóg now meet a physical object: a pingin of airgead. Imported types tháinig — came — into Dublin's visual world; the local issue chuaigh — went — out carrying a Dublin king and mint.
pages.detail: The past-tense pair enters through movement of a design and an object, not an unrelated travel drill.
pages.visualCaption: Generated editorial interpretation of light moving across a silver penny · not documentary evidence

pages.title: A die turns force into repeatable design
pages.body: A blank of silver was struck between engraved dies. The blow transferred portrait, cross and letters into relief. Variation in centring and strike is part of the object, not a manufacturing defect measured by modern machine standards.
pages.detail: The handling interaction can compare obverse and reverse without pretending to mint a documentary replica.

displayItems.title: Engraved dies
displayItems.detail: Type and legend cut in reverse

pages.title: The design speaks a familiar coin language
pages.body: The earliest Dublin issues imitate contemporary English pennies of Æthelred II. Imitation here is not a beginner's synonym for forgery. A recognisable type could make a new local issue legible within existing exchange networks.
pages.detail: The numismatist must select the exact learner-facing type before final copy names Crux or Long Cross details.

pages.title: One object page says 995; the series is dated more broadly
pages.body: The National Museum labels its Glendalough example as minted AD 995. Broader summaries place the first Dublin issues around 997 or 998. The draft keeps c. 995–997 visible until the selected specimen and catalogue convention are locked.
pages.detail: An exact year belongs to an identified object or catalogue argument, not to every coin in the phase.

pages.title: A diagram is not the chosen specimen
pages.body: The current app can show measured coin structure and legend zones without reproducing an uncleared museum image. Final production needs one named specimen, both faces, a catalogue reading and image rights. Until then, every detailed drawing remains provisional.
pages.detail: The rights and numismatics gates protect the object from becoming a generic Viking coin.

pages.title: The penny is made; now read its face
pages.body: Material, manufacture and type establish the coin as an object. Its sharpest county claim sits in the letters: a king and Dublin named on silver. The next chapter slows down enough to distinguish readable legend, expansion and portrait convention.
pages.detail: The story moves from how the penny was made to what it says.

chapters.title: Léigh an Finscéal · Read the legend

pages.title: The face carries king and city
pages.body: The pingin's earlier movement—tháinig and chuaigh—slows into inspection. Téigh means go; tar means come. On the provisional National Museum object, the learner goes to the obverse and comes back to a short claim: SITRIC REX DUBLIN.
pages.detail: The exact letter-by-letter legend and both-face catalogue reading remain behind the numismatist gate.
pages.visualCaption: Generated editorial interpretation of minting craft · not a documentary workshop record

pages.title: The head is a type, not a likeness
pages.body: The bust belongs to a recognised coin design derived from English models. It should not be presented as a documentary portrait of Sihtric's face. The legend identifies authority more securely than the image identifies appearance.
pages.detail: Portrait convention is part of coin literacy: a ruler type can stand for a king without preserving his features.

pages.title: A few letters carry a political sentence
pages.body: The legend compresses ainm, rí and cathair: Sihtric, king, Dublin. Spelling varies across specimens and catalogues, and the lettering may be abbreviated or uneven. Expansion turns a compact object text into a modern readable line.
pages.detail: The learning interaction reads the provisional object rather than teaching one spelling as universal across the series.

pages.title: Listen, then build the sentence
pages.context: Téigh go dtí an aghaidh; tar ar ais chuig an inscríbhinn
pages.body: Listen, then rebuild the complete instruction.

exercise.objective: Hear téigh and tar in an object-inspection instruction.
exercise.prompt: Listen, then put the words in order.
exercise.answer: Téigh go dtí an aghaidh; tar ar ais chuig an inscríbhinn.
exercise.translation: Go to the face; come back to the inscription.
exercise.audioText: Téigh go dtí an aghaidh; tar ar ais chuig an inscríbhinn.
exercise.modelText: Téigh go dtí an aghaidh; tar ar ais chuig an inscríbhinn.
exercise.feedback: The movement verbs now organise close inspection rather than generic travel.
exercise.hint: Téigh begins the outward action; tar ar ais begins the return.
exercise.recovery: Keep go dtí an aghaidh in the first clause.

pages.title: The reverse matters to identification
pages.body: A complete numismatic reading uses both sides: type, legend, moneyer and mint signature. The current draft does not assign a reverse legend until the numismatist confirms the exact object. A one-face story would be visually simple and evidentially incomplete.
pages.detail: The final interface must allow obverse–reverse comparison with one stable specimen record.

pages.title: The eye needs a path around a circle
pages.body: Coin text does not read like a line on a page. Letters turn around the edge, may be clipped by the strike and continue beside images. A good learner view rotates or segments the legend without redrawing the coin into false neatness.
pages.detail: The interaction teaches how to inspect a small circular source, not merely what answer to select.

pages.title: Tap the matching pairs
pages.body: Connect the three visible units to what they name.

exercise.objective: Connect the provisional legend units to ruler, role and city.
exercise.prompt: Match each unit to its meaning.
exercise.answer: all pairs
exercise.feedback: Name, king and city form the penny's compact public claim.
exercise.hint: REX is the title; DUBLIN is the city.
exercise.recovery: Those two roles do not match. Try another unit.

pages.title: The museum title is enough for a draft, not final cataloguing
pages.body: The National Museum page supplies a named object, a date, an identification and a relationship to Æthelred's design. Final production still needs the numismatist's chosen transcription, series classification and disposition of any mismatch between page title and visible letters.
pages.detail: The pack keeps a usable reading while refusing to pretend specialist cataloguing has happened.

pages.title: Complete the return instruction
pages.body: Choose the verb that brings the learner back to the legend.

exercise.objective: Use tar in a complete movement phrase.
exercise.prompt: Complete: ___ ar ais chuig an ainm.
exercise.answer: Tar

options.text: Tar
Téigh
Chuaigh

exercise.translation: Come back to the name.
exercise.modelText: Tar ar ais chuig an ainm.
exercise.feedback: Tar ar ais chuig an ainm — come back to the name.
exercise.hint: Choose the verb meaning come.
exercise.recovery: Téigh moves away; tar brings the learner back.

pages.title: Choose what the face can support
pages.body: Distinguish authority from likeness and universal spelling.

exercise.objective: Identify the bounded meaning of the provisional legend.
exercise.prompt: What does the legend support most directly?
exercise.answer: The issue names Sihtric as king and connects him to Dublin.

options.text: The issue names Sihtric as king and connects him to Dublin.
options.rationale: This is the bounded legend claim.

options.text: The bust records Sihtric's exact face.
options.rationale: It is a conventional ruler type.

options.text: Every early Dublin penny has identical letters.

exercise.feedback: The letters support a named authority and city.
exercise.hint: Choose what letters can establish without treating the bust as a portrait.
exercise.recovery: A coin type cannot prove exact facial appearance or one spelling across every specimen.

pages.title: The city can travel in a pocket
pages.body: Once the penny names ruler and city, every movement becomes part of the claim's afterlife. The final chapter follows one museum object away from Dublin to its discovery at Glendalough and asks what such travel can—and cannot—tell us.
pages.detail: Reading the legend makes the object's later findspot meaningful.

pages.title: Build the sentence
pages.context: Téigh chuig an ainm; tar ar ais chuig an rí agus an chathair
pages.body: Use both movement verbs with the legend's three claims.

exercise.objective: Produce téigh and tar while reusing ainm, rí and cathair.
exercise.prompt: Build: Go to the name; come back to the king and city.
exercise.answer: Téigh chuig an ainm; tar ar ais chuig an rí agus an chathair.
exercise.translation: Go to the name; come back to the king and city.
exercise.modelText: Téigh chuig an ainm; tar ar ais chuig an rí agus an chathair.
exercise.feedback: The sentence turns legend reading into an ordered movement.
exercise.hint: Build the téigh clause first, then tar ar ais.
exercise.recovery: Keep chuig after each movement phrase.

chapters.title: Turas na Pingine · The penny travels

pages.title: A Dublin penny surfaces at Glendalough
pages.body: The National Museum's named penny was found at Glendalough. It tháinig from a Dublin minting world and chuaigh beyond the city before entering the archaeological record. Téigh and tar return as evidence verbs: go from issue to findspot, then come back to the claims on the coin.
pages.detail: A documented find gives the object a later location without supplying every step of its journey.
pages.visualCaption: Generated editorial interpretation of riverfront archaeology · not a documentary find photo

pages.title: The distance is real; the route is missing
pages.body: A find away from the mint proves that the object moved. It does not tell us who carried it, how many exchanges it passed through or whether it travelled soon after striking. The blank middle of the route is part of the evidence.
pages.detail: The app must not cast the learner as the coin's owner or invent a continuous itinerary.

pages.title: The issue opens a thousand-year coin story
pages.body: The first Dublin pennies begin a local minting history that later changes rulers, types, places and metals. Their importance does not come from being primitive. They show a mature port adopting a familiar technology to make local authority legible.
pages.detail: The afterlife page connects the object to Irish coin history without racing through later centuries.

pages.title: Notice came and went
pages.body: Choose the line that keeps the directions correct.

exercise.objective: Distinguish the two supported past forms in the object's route.
exercise.prompt: Which line means: The penny came from Dublin and went to Glendalough?
exercise.answer: Tháinig an phingin ó Bhaile Átha Cliath agus chuaigh sí go Gleann Dá Loch.

options.text: Tháinig an phingin ó Bhaile Átha Cliath agus chuaigh sí go Gleann Dá Loch.
Chuaigh an phingin ó Gleann Dá Loch agus tháinig sí go Baile Átha Cliath.
options.rationale: This reverses the documented mint and find places.

options.text: Téigh an phingin agus tar sí.
options.rationale: These are instruction forms, not the supported past account.

exercise.translation: The penny came from Dublin and went to Glendalough.
exercise.modelText: Tháinig an phingin ó Bhaile Átha Cliath agus chuaigh sí go Gleann Dá Loch.
exercise.feedback: Tháinig brings the penny from Dublin; chuaigh sends it onward.
exercise.hint: The line must use tháinig before chuaigh.
exercise.recovery: The other lines reverse the directions or use present-tense movement.

pages.title: The collection keeps object and interpretation apart
pages.context: What survives · what the learner carries
pages.body: The museum object belongs under What survives, with its accession number, findspot, date and provisional reading. A learner-made legend rubbing or coin diagram belongs under What you made. The twenty words belong under Words you carry only after Learning mode is complete.
pages.detail: The closing handoff preserves the product's evidence boundary.

pages.title: Speak the supported journey
pages.context: Chuaigh an phingin ón gcathair go Gleann Dá Loch
pages.body: Record the route without inventing its missing carrier.

exercise.objective: Produce chuaigh, pingin and cathair in a complete evidence sentence.
exercise.prompt: Record: Chuaigh an phingin ón gcathair go Gleann Dá Loch.
exercise.answer: Chuaigh an phingin ón gcathair go Gleann Dá Loch.
exercise.translation: The penny went from the city to Glendalough.
exercise.audioText: Chuaigh an phingin ón gcathair go Gleann Dá Loch.
exercise.modelText: Chuaigh an phingin ón gcathair go Gleann Dá Loch.
exercise.feedback: The line states movement between known places and leaves the carrier unknown.
exercise.hint: Keep an phingin together after chuaigh.
exercise.recovery: If recording is unavailable, replay the model and continue without saving audio.

pages.title: What this county account can claim
pages.body: The account can show an established port, Sihtric's authority, the first local issues, the borrowed design language, a provisional legend and one excavated find. It cannot recover the mint decree, universal use, exact portrait or the coin's continuous route.
pages.detail: Each confident claim remains tied to the object or official museum synthesis that supports it.

pages.title: Tap the matching pairs
pages.body: Reconnect the minted object to the world that made it useful.

exercise.objective: Connect three county anchors to their meanings.
exercise.prompt: Match each Irish word to its meaning.
exercise.answer: all pairs
exercise.feedback: Penny, trade and city remain one account rather than three vocabulary cards.
exercise.hint: The pingin moves through trádáil in the cathair.
exercise.recovery: Those two do not match. Try the remaining meaning.

pages.title: Choose the complete Dublin claim
pages.body: Keep the strongest account and its missing middle together.

exercise.objective: Identify the evidence-grounded county summary.
exercise.prompt: Which summary can this pack support?
exercise.answer: A connected Dublin port struck early silver pennies under Sihtric; a named example carries king and city and later appears at Glendalough.

options.text: A connected Dublin port struck early silver pennies under Sihtric; a named example carries king and city and later appears at Glendalough.
options.rationale: This is the bounded county account.

options.text: A surviving decree records why Sihtric founded the mint.
options.rationale: No such decree anchors the story.

options.text: The coin records every owner between Dublin and Glendalough.

exercise.feedback: The summary joins place, ruler, object, text and findspot without inventing motive or route.
exercise.hint: Choose the account tied to the museum object and the local-coinage synthesis.
exercise.recovery: The other answers claim a royal speech or a complete travel diary.

pages.title: Carry a city in a few letters
pages.body: Dublin closes with a compact achievement: the learner can move from port to king, from market to mint, from silver to legend and from issue to findspot. The penny enters the collection as evidence; its words enter review only through Learning completion.
pages.detail: Story completion opens the next county without making a language claim.

pages.title: Bring the port and penny together
pages.context: Tháinig airgead chuig an gcathair; chuaigh pingin ón mionta chuig an margadh
pages.body: Retrieve the county's material, city, object and movement in one line.

exercise.objective: Produce a closing sentence reusing five county anchors.
exercise.prompt: Type: Silver came to the city; a penny went from the mint to the market.
exercise.answer: Tháinig airgead chuig an gcathair; chuaigh pingin ón mionta chuig an margadh.
exercise.translation: Silver came to the city; a penny went from the mint to the market.
exercise.modelText: Tháinig airgead chuig an gcathair; chuaigh pingin ón mionta chuig an margadh.
exercise.feedback: The final line carries the material into Dublin and the issued object out.
exercise.hint: Use tháinig in the first clause and chuaigh in the second.
exercise.recovery: Keep ón mionta with the penny's outward movement.
